transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-31 15:30 PDT | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (DataHarbor Head of ML), Tom Reyes (DataHarbor SRE), Leah Park (DataHarbor CTO)

[00:00] Alex: yep okay um, thanks everyone for joining. we have about 55 minutes. today's goal is to align on the benchmark plan, what you need to run your scripts in the harness, and the success criteria.
[00:18] Maya: thanks Alex, yeah excited. we want to validate both streaming and non-streaming paths, because we surface responses to users as streaming in prod but our batch offline jobs hit non-streaming endpoints.
[00:35] Priya: mm-hmm, makes sense. quick question on sample sizes — what's your typical RPS and tokens per request in prod?
[00:48] Maya: in prod at peak we see about 120 rps across the service, avg token count around 350 tokens per request, heavy tails up to 1.2k tokens on large docs. for the POC we can simulate three tiers: baseline 50 rps, ramp to 150 rps, and a stress at 300 rps.
[01:10] Tom: add to that, our concurrency at the application tier is about 250 connections; we care about p95 latency and also sustained throughput per GPU.
[01:25] Priya: okay good, that's very helpful. for the harness we usually run scenarios that mirror those tiers. for streaming vs non-streaming, streaming increases per-connection overhead but reduces perceived latency. non-streaming gives better token throughput per GPU.
[01:43] Alex: can we write down success criteria? suggested from Redwood side: streaming p95 < 350ms for typical 350-token requests, non-streaming end-to-end latency < 800ms for same payload, and throughput target of >= 150 rps sustained with 95% token completion and error rate < 0.5% during test.
[02:05] Leah: those sound reasonable. need to confirm with execs but generally yes. also we want a cost projection — tokens per second and approximate dollars per million tokens at the config you test.
[02:20] Priya: we'll provide a throughput vs cost table after the initial runs. one thing to note: quantized model variants change latency/cost profiles; do you have preference on model family?
[02:33] Maya: we prefer an open model close to Llama2 family for licencing reasons; we can test both fp16 and 4-bit quantized variants if Redwood supports that in the harness.
[02:45] Jordan: we do support quantized variants in the runtime; for the harness we'll label configs so you can compare apples-to-apples.
[02:55] Tom: about the harness integration — our team has existing load scripts in Python and k6. we want to reuse those rather than rewrite them. how does Redwood accept customer scripts?
[03:08] Priya: two options: 1) you point us to the scripts repo and we adapt a small wrapper to call the harness runner, or 2) you drop a small shim (we have a template) that conforms to our harness interface. option 1 is usually faster for us to onboard.
[03:22] Maya: option 1 preferred. we'll share a repo link with sample payloads and auth tokens (test tokens).
[03:31] Alex: perfect. Maya, can you share the traffic profile, i.e. distribution of token lengths and percent of streaming vs non-streaming requests?
[03:40] Maya: yes — roughly 70% streaming, 30% non-streaming. token length distribution: 60% small <200, 30% mid 200-600, 10% large >600.
[03:55] Priya: great, we'll create CI configs for those weighted mixes. for streaming tests we run both chunked streaming and single-shot streaming to represent different front-end implementations.
[04:08] Tom: on the network/security side — we need VPC peering for Private deployment tests; for Hosted we require inbound IP allowlist for the harness load runners. we also need SOC2 + SSO docs.
[04:21] Alex: we'll attach SOC2 + encryption/KMS docs; for SSO we support SAML and OIDC. for VPC peering we'll coordinate maintenance windows — what times work for you?
[04:31] Tom: weekday evenings PST is preferred, but we can schedule a window the week of Apr 6.
[04:38] Leah: also confirm audit logging — we need request-level logs exported to our SIEM for the pilot.
[04:46] Jordan: we emit request traces and token-level billing metrics; we can hook to your log ingestion via secure transfer. will confirm the exact fields.
[04:55] Maya: on success criteria beyond latency — we want no regressions in output quality. we'll run a small eval set of 200 prompts and expect match/score thresholds; if quality drops with quantization that's a failure mode.
[05:10] Priya: we've set up regression eval harnesses before; please share the prompts and grading criteria. we can run automatic comparisons and report differences.
[05:22] Alex: timeline suggestion: share scripts and traffic profile by Apr 2, Redwood preps harness configs and sends them by Apr 3, initial dry run Apr 6, full load run April 7-8, analysis by Apr 9 and cost/throughput report Apr 10. does that align?
[05:40] Maya: yes that aligns with our internal deadlines.
[05:45] Tom: couple of technical clarifications — for streaming latency measurements do you measure time to first token or time to last token?
[05:52] Priya: we measure both. time-to-first-token (TTFT) for perceived latency and last-token completion for correctness and throughput accounting. we'll report p50/p95 for TTFT and overall completion latency.
[06:05] Tom: for the harness runners, what's the recommended concurrency model? our current scripts open persistent connections for streaming; for non-streaming we spin up separate HTTP clients.
[06:18] Priya: keep the persistent connections for streaming to simulate production; for non-streaming we recommend ramping virtual users to hit target RPS. we'll provide a k6 example for both patterns.
[06:30] Alex: let's talk about metrics to collect in the report: p50/p95 TTFT, p50/p95 completion latency, tokens/sec per GPU, error rates, CPU/GPU utilization, cache hit rates if KV cache used, and cost estimate.
[06:47] Maya: can you also include tail latency percentiles up to p99? our SLOs are strict there.
[06:54] Priya: yes we'll include p99 and a heatmap of latency by token length bucket.
[07:02] Jordan: regarding KV cache — if your workload has repeated prefixes we can enable prefix caching; that'll materially improve throughput for short-turn dialogues. is that relevant?
[07:14] Maya: some flows are repeated templates so caching likely helps; we'll flag which endpoints are template-based.
[07:22] Tom: about model variants and fallbacks — if the dedicated capacity is exhausted can Redwood automatically route to a cheaper hosted variant? that impacts cost reporting.
[07:32] Alex: yes we have policy-based routing but for the POC we should pin capacity to avoid routing variability. we'll simulate fallback separately.
[07:42] Maya: regarding data retention and logs, what's Redwood's retention default? we need 90 days of audit logs for the pilot.
[07:50] Alex: default is 30 days; we can enable 90 days as an add-on for the POC and export logs to your SIEM. we'll include the cost implications in the report.
[07:59] Tom: ok. on the harness side — our k6 scripts call your endpoint using an API key; do you support per-run test keys to isolate usage?
[08:08] Priya: yes we generate ephemeral keys for test runs and we can tag them to your account for cost attribution.
[08:16] Maya: good. security checklist: SOC2, SSO integration, KMS for encryption at rest, VPC peering, ephemeral test keys, and audit log export. anything else?
[08:29] Alex: that's the main list. we'll attach the security pack to the follow-up email.
[08:35] Jordan: a practical note — for large token requests (1k+ tokens) we recommend testing with larger effective batch sizes; the harness will run both single-request and batched modes to show throughput tradeoffs.
[08:47] Maya: we definitely want batched tests to see cost per token improvement.
[08:52] Priya: noted. we'll include a batched vs unbatched comparison in the report.
[08:58] Tom: for the test machine footprint, what GPU types will the hosted harness use? we want to correlate tokens/sec to specific GPU models.
[09:07] Alex: initial runs will use NVIDIA H100-like instances for parity, and we'll also provide data for A100 and a quantized low-cost variant (T4/RTX-class equivalent). we'll label each result with instance type.
[09:21] Leah: budget question — we need a very rough cost range for the pilot. can you give a ballpark?
[09:28] Alex: ballpark depends on total tokens for the run; we'll estimate after the first dry run but preliminary estimate is a few thousand dollars for the initial load runs, we'll refine in the Apr 10 report.
[09:40] Maya: one more thing — latency variance across regions. we operate in US-West primarily but would like one run from EU to check egress behavior.
[09:50] Priya: we can spin runners in EU region as well and tag results by region.
[10:00] Alex: great. any blockers from DataHarbor side?
[10:04] Maya: just internal approvals on the execs and making sure we can share the sample data (sanitized).
[10:10] Tom: on our side we need the peering window scheduled.
[10:14] Alex: okay next steps recap — Alex sends harness repo + security pack, Priya sends example k6 configs and streaming shims, Maya provides scripts and traffic profile, Tom confirms peering window. then we run dry run Apr 6 and full runs Apr 7-8.
[10:33] Leah: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[10:36] Alex: thanks, we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the runs and the repo link.
[10:40] Maya: thanks all.
[54:50] [meeting end]
